title: Wind geography: a world that finally has sheltered places in it
question: Do the dark bands land where you would expect shelter — in the lee of ridges and down in hollows — and does the bright/dark difference look strong enough to be worth a tree growing differently for? Separately: every gust in the world is now 35–100% of its old strength, so the whole world is about a third calmer. Is that acceptable, or should sheltered ground be the only thing that changes?
context_md:
`weather::at(seed, frame)` **took no position** — wind was one number for the entire world, so a hollow and an exposed ridge got identical weather and there was no such thing as a sheltered spot.

`exposure(terrain, position)` is a **read-only** function: open fetch upwind plus height above the local terrain. It writes nothing to the field, stores nothing, wakes no chunk — which is the whole line between it and the steady-wind term that was measured at a permanent 3.55 ms/scene and reverted four times.

**Both panels are the same world** (`preset=rolling seed=7`), same frame, so the geography and the reading line up column for column. Wind is from the west, so shelter falls to the **right** of each ridge.

The ramp is fixed, not per-frame: deep navy = sheltered, mid slate = level open ground, pale straw = fully exposed. The cyan line is the terrain surface. Control: `preset=flat` reads a uniform 0.500, spread 0.000.

Cost: **no measurable frame cost** — `ascii` organism scene, re-measured back to back this session, main mean 4.640 ms vs branch 4.589 ms.
